title: Crocheting with mohair and fuzzy yarns
subtitle: Handling hairy and brushed fibres that obscure the stitches
excerpt: Mohair, brushed alpaca, and other fuzzy yarns are worked the same way as smooth yarns but the halo of fibres around each stitch makes it difficult to see stitch heads and insert the hook accurately. Working more slowly, using good lighting, and choosing appropriate hook sizes and stitch patterns makes fuzzy yarn manageable. The halo also makes mistakes harder to frog, which is a practical reason to keep tension even from the start.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: The cloud of fine fibres that surrounds the core of a mohair or brushed-alpaca yarn after knitting or crocheting. The halo obscures stitch definition but produces a soft, airy fabric.

Unravelling crocheted fabric made from mohair or other hairy fibres. Significantly harder than frogging smooth yarn because the halo fibres tangle around adjacent stitches and often snap rather than releasing cleanly.

content.text: is the defining quality of mohair and brushed-alpaca yarn: a cloud of fine, soft fibres extends beyond the core and wraps around adjacent stitches as you work. This creates beautiful softness and drape in the finished fabric, but makes stitch insertion harder and
painful. Working carefully the first time is far preferable to ripping back several rows of mohair.
Hook size and stitch choice for fuzzy yarns

Mohair is often used at a much larger hook than its core weight suggests. A fine mohair or kid mohair (similar in core thickness to lace weight) is commonly worked on a 6.0 to 7.0 mm hook to produce a light, airy fabric where the halo floats between open stitches. Treble crochet and double treble open meshes work well with mohair because the open stitch structure lets the halo bloom without creating a dense fabric.
Tips for working with fuzzy yarns
Work in good light. The stitch heads of mohair are hard to see; side lighting that casts small shadows in the V of each stitch makes them much easier to find.
Use a smooth, low-friction hook. The mohair fibres catch on rough hooks and on matte-finished hook shafts. A smooth aluminium or polished steel hook releases the yarn more cleanly.

Count stitches at the end of every row. It is easy to accidentally work two stitches into the same chain space or to skip a stitch when the stitch tops are obscured. Catching errors early limits how much must be unravelled.
Use a stitch marker in the first and last stitch of each row so the edge stitches are easy to locate.
Work at a relaxed pace. The fibres need time to release cleanly as you draw each loop through; rushing causes them to catch and bunch.

items.symptom: It is impossible to find the stitch heads to insert the hook
items.cause: The halo is hiding the stitch top completely.
items.fix: Gently separate the halo fibres with your fingertip to find the two top loops. Use the tip of a darning needle or a crochet hook tip to locate the V before inserting the working hook.

items.symptom: The yarn is breaking when attempting to frog a row
items.cause: Mohair fibres tangle together and create resistance when unravelling; pulling too hard snaps the fine core yarn.
items.fix: Frog very slowly, one stitch at a time, using the hook to gently lift each stitch off the previous one. Accept that frogging mohair is slow. More than two or three rows can be effectively impossible to frog cleanly.

items.symptom: The fabric looks patchy and uneven due to inconsistent halo distribution
items.cause: Tension varies between rows, compressing the halo in tight rows and opening it in loose rows.
items.fix: Aim for consistent tension across all rows. Even tension distributes the halo evenly; the halo then blooms uniformly and covers any minor stitch irregularities.

content.text: Work a 10 cm by 10 cm swatch in treble crochet on a large hook (try 6.5 mm for a fine mohair). The open mesh lets the halo spread evenly and demonstrates how mohair in an open stitch pattern produces its characteristic light, airy look that makes it popular for wraps and shawls.
